name: Marrow Frequency Collective
description:
Founded in 2208 by retired pipe-fitter and amateur sound engineer Dagny Osei-Watanabe out of a converted water-treatment substation in the Circuit's Kazan District, Marrow Frequency Collective is a worker-owned independent label operating on stubbornness, mutual aid, and a secondhand pressing lathe that breaks down every three months. The label's founding charter — still posted on the wall of the substation in laminated print — states that no artist on the roster will surrender catalog rights, no release will carry a compliance certification from any Vantablack subsidiary, and all net revenue above operating costs will be split equally between the artist and the Collective's infrastructure fund. These principles have kept MFC perpetually underfunded and perpetually alive.

The Collective releases music on data chips, vinyl pressed in-house, and through an encrypted mesh node maintained by a rotating crew of volunteer technicians who have never all been in the same room simultaneously for security reasons. Neural-feed distribution exists but is unlicensed — technically gray market, operating through borrowed bandwidth and mesh handshakes that Vantablack's compliance monitors haven't yet been configured to catch. The roster leans heavily toward Circuit blues, Shelf-adjacent protest, and what the label calls 'stratum folk' — music that deals honestly with the lived experience of working-class GLMZ without romanticizing it.
creator: Dagny Osei-Watanabe (founding director, 2208–present)
genre: Circuit blues, Stratum folk, Shelf protest, Working-class neural folk
audience: Tier 1 and Tier 2 workers, labor organizers, independent music communities across the Circuit, Tier 3 listeners who seek out unlicensed distribution
cultural_impact: In a city where independent labels are routinely acquired, litigated out of existence, or simply starved of distribution bandwidth by Vantablack's infrastructure monopoly, MFC's survival is itself a political act. The Collective has become a quiet symbol for labor organizers and mutual-aid networks — not because its music is explicitly political (though some of it is) but because its structure is. Several Circuit labor guilds have adopted MFC releases as de facto anthems without any formal arrangement, simply because the music was already playing in their meeting halls. Vantablack's legal division has sent three cease-and-desist letters regarding unlicensed mesh distribution; all three are also laminated and posted on the substation wall.
known_fans: Shelf musicians who aspire to fair deals
story_hooks: Dagny Osei-Watanabe has received a fourth legal notice — this one not a cease-and-desist but a full civil asset seizure filing. Vantablack's legal team has found a technical violation in the substation's original lease. The Collective has three weeks and almost no Φ. Someone needs to find out if the lease violation is real or manufactured, and if manufactured, who inside city records was paid to alter it.

One of MFC's volunteer mesh technicians has gone missing two days before a major encrypted data-chip release. The release contains an album with lyrics that name specific Vantablack compliance officers by pseudonym. Whether the disappearance is coincidence or warning, the remaining volunteers are divided on whether to proceed.

A Tier 4 music lawyer approaches MFC with a genuine offer: pro bono legal defense and a clean distribution license, in exchange for the Collective taking on one artist — a Spire-adjacent musician who claims to have been blacklisted by Vantablack and wants to release through an independent. Dagny suspects a setup. The artist's music is undeniably good.
